1:
The witnesses open the chapter on two fronts at once — the reckoning of its date and the temper of the people it gathers. The reformed John Gill fixes the season: the seventh month is Tisri, answering to part of September and October, though he prefers to read that it "was approaching," since certain things were done before it had fully come, the people meeting and an altar rising so that on its first day sacrifice might be offered. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the intervening months: the exiles had left Babylon about the spring, and on reaching Jerusalem threw up huts and sheds among the ruins to lodge in, so that some months passed before, as the month came round, they reared the altar and kept the feast of tabernacles, offering sacrifices as regularly as though the temple were standing.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the architecture of the whole chapter from this verse: on the approach of the seventh month the people assembled to restore the altar and the sacrificial worship and to keep the feast (vv.1-7), and in the following year the foundations of the temple were laid (vv.8-13). The year, they note, is unstated but is the year of the return, as v.8 shows; and the clause "the children of Israel were in the cities" is a circumstantial note reaching back to Ezra 2:70. Charles Ellicott adds that Tisri, answering to September, was the most solemn month of the year, holding the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles — later called "the feast" pre-eminently — and that "as one man" means not all, but with one consent.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the bare notice into a portrait of zeal. He supposes the people came from Babylon in the spring, allowing four months for so long a journey, as Ezra's own company took (Ezra 7:9); the seventh month soon came with its feasts, and they gathered themselves by agreement among themselves rather than by any command of authority. Though newly returned, with their hands full of providing for their families, such was their zeal that they left all their business in the country to attend God's altar — and, strange to say, in this pious zeal they were all of a mind, coming "as one man." Let worldly business, Henry urges, be postponed to the business of religion, and it will prosper the better. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees the month was a sacred one, full of festivals for which the people had prepared. The witnesses do not divide; together they set the frame — a returned remnant, still homeless among ruins, choosing worship before comfort.
2:
The rebuilding begins not with walls but with an altar, and the witnesses gather around the two men who raised it. The reformed John Gill names first Jeshua the son of Jozadak, the high priest, the proper person to give the lead in the work; and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies his pedigree, that he was grandson of Seraiah the high priest whom Nebuchadnezzar had put to death (2 Kings 25:18), so that this Jeshua was the first high priest after the captivity — the priesthood taking up again, in the grandson, the office broken off in the grandfather's execution.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set beside him Zerubbabel the prince, and read the verse as the joining of the two leaders with their brethren — the priests and the men of Israel, clergy and laity together — to build the altar and offer burnt-offerings upon it, as prescribed in the law of Moses, that is, to restore the legal sacrifices. They reason from the sequel that since the offering began on the first day of the seventh month (v.6), the altar must have been finished by that day, which agrees exactly with the notice that the work was done as the seventh month "approached." Charles Ellicott sharpens the point that the altar was built "only as the beginning of their work"; the temple was, as it were, to be built around the altar as the centre of all. And "Moses the man of God," he observes, is the honorific given him as it is given David, citing Nehemiah 12:24.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out why the altar came first. It was of more present necessity than the temple, he says, on three grounds: to make atonement to God for all their sins, to obtain God's assistance for the great work of building the temple, and to strengthen their own hearts and hands for it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, surveying the same scene, draws the lessons the leaders' haste teaches. First, to begin with God: the more difficult and necessitous our case, the more concerned we are to take him along with us in all our ways; if we would be directed by his oracles, let him be honoured by our offerings. And second, to do what we can in the worship of God when we cannot do what we would — they could not immediately have a temple, but they would not be without an altar; as Abraham, wherever he came, built an altar, so we, though we may want the benefit of preaching and the eucharist, are wanting in our duty if we bring not the sacrifices of prayer and praise, for we have an altar that sanctifies the gift. The witnesses do not divide; they read the altar as the returned people's confession that all rebuilding must begin at the place of atonement.
3:
Two things hold the witnesses' attention here — where the altar was set, and the fear that hurried its raising. On the first, the reformed John Gill takes "they set the altar upon his bases" to mean it was fixed on the same spot where it had stood before, upon what might remain of the old altar. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch prefer to render it "upon its former place" rather than "upon its bases," treating the noun as a form of the word for a fixed site (as at Ezra 2:68) and judging the alternative pointing of the text an incorrect revision. Charles Ellicott joins them: the altar was reared upon its old site, its place discovered among the ruins, and by this it was signified that all the new was to be only a restoration of the old.

The fear draws the deeper comment. Keil and Delitzsch explain the Hebrew idiom — a "being in fear" had come upon them — and identify "the people of those countries" as the surrounding heathen population, the same neighbours named at Ezra 9:1 and Ezra 10:2; they set up the altar and restored the worship of the LORD precisely to secure the divine protection, because dread of those nations had fallen on them. Ellicott reads the same motive from the inside: until their offerings went up they did not feel sure of the divine protection, and this was their first act of defiance in the presence of the nations round about — for near the altar they were strong. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that they reared the altar to keep up the divine worship during the rebuilding, and did so "though fear was upon them," because of the unfriendly disposition of their neighbours.

The witnesses do not divide, but two readings of the fear's effect run side by side. Ellicott and Clarke stress that though they were afraid, yet they built the altar, refusing to be frightened from their religion by the opposition they were likely to meet. John Wesley presses the other edge: because they were afraid, therefore they made the more haste, lest they should be hindered — and he turns it into a rule, that apprehension of dangers should quicken us in our duty; have we many enemies, then we have the more need to have God for our friend, and to keep up our correspondence with him. The two emphases are not contradictory but complementary: the fear that might have driven a weaker people from the altar drove this one to it, and the offering of morning and evening sacrifice, begun in the midst of enemies, became the returned remnant's boldest confession that their safety lay not in walls but in the God whose worship they had restored.
4:
With the altar standing, the remnant keeps the first of the great feasts, and the witnesses read the feast of tabernacles as the deliberate reopening of the whole Mosaic order of worship. The reformed John Gill notes that they kept it "as it is written," according to the rules prescribed for its observance, beginning on the fifteenth day of the seventh month. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm that it was kept as the law directs (Leviticus 23:34), and unfold the odd phrase "the burnt offerings day by day by number": these are the sacrifices commanded for the several days of the festival — on the first day thirteen oxen, on the second twelve, and so descending — exactly as laid down in Numbers 29:13-34, the "duty of every day required" being counted out beast by beast.

Charles Ellicott presses the theological point that the verse is built to make. To grasp the phrase "according to the custom," he says, one must read together Deuteronomy 16, Leviticus 23, and Numbers 29; the intention is plainly to lay stress on the provision now being made for an entire renewal of the Mosaic economy of service — a renewal the next verse will spell out in full. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the same chronology, that the feast began on the fifteenth day, though the regular offerings had been kept from the first day of the month (v.6), and were religiously continued all the while the temple was building.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley raises the one difficulty the verse leaves. The feast of tabernacles, he suggests, seems to be named for all the solemnities of that month, as the most eminent of them; for otherwise it is not probable that they would have neglected the Day of Atonement, so severely enjoined in Leviticus 23:27-29 and so exceedingly suitable to their present condition. Matthew Henry, surveying the same feast, had drawn out its fitness: now that they had received such great mercy, that joyful feast was in a special manner seasonable, and now that they were beginning to settle in their cities it might well remind them of their fathers' dwelling in tents in the wilderness; the feast that had a peculiar reference to gospel times, as Zechariah 14:18 shows, was brought into special reputation as those times drew on. The witnesses do not divide; together they read the feast as the returned people's reentry into the appointed round of Israel's worship, the whole law taken up again where it had so long lain silent.
5:
The verse gathers the ordinary and the occasional sacrifices into one list, and the witnesses attend chiefly to the order in which they were offered. The reformed John Gill guards against a misreading: the continual burnt offering was not something begun only after the feast of tabernacles, for the daily sacrifice had been set going as soon as the altar was reared, on the first day of the month; rather the sense is that after the daily morning burnt offering they offered the other sacrifices peculiar to the several days, the daily oblation never neglected but always taken first, all the rest coming after it, and so likewise on the other festivals.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the sequence the same way: after the feast of tabernacles they offered the continual — that is, the daily — burnt-offering, and the offerings for the new moon, and those of all the appointed festivals of the LORD, the annual feasts. The freewill offering they define precisely: a nedabah is a burnt-offering brought from free inclination, which might be presented on any day but was chiefly offered at the annual festivals, after the sacrifices the law prescribed, as Numbers 29:39 provides. Charles Ellicott takes the whole verse as general and anticipatory: the new moons, the three great feasts, and the constant presentation of freewill offerings, added to the daily sacrifice, made up the essentials of the ritual — all of them, like the arrangements in the book of Leviticus, fixed and observed before ever the temple was built.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fastens on the freewill offerings for a lesson in devotion. The continual burnt offering he takes for the morning and evening sacrifice; and then he marvels at the freewill offerings each man brought, for "the law required much, but they offered more; for though they had little wealth, they had much zeal." Happy are they, he adds, who bring with them out of the furnace of affliction such a holy heat as this. Matthew Henry had drawn out the same wonder: the law required much, but they brought more, and though they had little wealth to support the expense of their sacrifices, they had much zeal, and, we may suppose, spared at their own tables that they might plentifully supply God's altar. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch fix the careful order — the daily offering first, the special sacrifices after; Ellicott the completeness of a ritual restored before the house was standing; Wesley and Henry the open-handedness of an impoverished people who gave beyond the letter of the law. Together they render a portrait of worship at once exact and generous, obedient to the smallest rubric and yet running past it in gratitude.
6:
This verse is largely a note of time, and the witnesses read it as the historian's own summary and hinge. The reformed John Gill marks the significance of the date: from the first of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings, and that first day was no ordinary one, being both a new moon and a grand festival, the feast of blowing of trumpets (Leviticus 23:24); and he has no doubt they also kept the tenth day of the month with all its rites, the solemn Day of Atonement (Leviticus 23:27). Charles Ellicott spells out the "notes of time" the verse turns on: the altar was raised before the month itself had come, and from the first day of the month until the fifteenth, when the feast of tabernacles began, the daily sacrifice was offered — so that the whole verse recapitulates what has gone before, its latter part serving as the transition to what follows.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse the same way, as a supplementary remark: the sacrificial worship began from the first day of the seventh month, but the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid — a clause that deliberately looks forward, opening the door to the account of the foundation-laying that fills the rest of the chapter. The sacrifices were restored at once; the house would wait until the spring. That gap between a functioning altar and an unbuilt temple is the very thing the verse is written to record.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley attends to the single phrase "burnt offerings." By it he understands not only the burnt offerings strictly so called but the other sacrifices that were to be offered along with them on that day, it being the feast of trumpets; for "burnt offerings," he observes, are often put in Scripture for all sacrifices whatever. The witnesses do not divide, and the sparse verse gains its weight from its place. It stands as a deliberate pause: the returned remnant has, in a matter of weeks, rebuilt the altar, resumed the daily sacrifice, and kept the appointed feasts of the seventh month, and yet — the verse insists — the temple itself is not so much as begun. The distance between the two facts is the measure of both their zeal and their poverty. They would not delay the worship of God for want of a house; but neither could they yet raise the house their fathers had lost. The altar goes up in an autumn; the foundation must wait, as the following verses will tell, for the second month of the second year — and the historian, by this careful accounting of days, binds the two seasons of the work together.
7:
With the worship restored, the remnant turns to the material preparation for the house itself, and the witnesses read the verse against the great precedent of Solomon. The reformed John Gill notes plainly that they gave money to the masons and to the carpenters, to purchase stone and timber for the building of the temple. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sees in the whole procedure a deliberate copying of Solomon's conduct while he built the first temple (1 Kings 5:11): as Solomon had employed the Tyrians and given them meat and drink, so now the returned Jews, having the same permission from Cyrus, hire the same Phoenician craftsmen and supply them in kind.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fill in the arrangement and its logistics. Keil and Delitzsch describe how money was given to the hewers of wood and the masons, and meat and drink — that is, corn and wine — and oil to the men of Sidon and Tyre, the Phoenicians (as at 1 Chronicles 22:4), to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea of Joppa, exactly as had been done in Solomon's day (1 Kings 5:6; 2 Chronicles 2:7), and all this according to the grant they had of Cyrus. Charles Ellicott marks the nice distinction the verse preserves: the Jews' own workmen were paid in money, but the Phoenicians, as in Solomon's days, were paid in kind — a practice, he notes, that both illustrates and is illustrated by the men of Tyre and Sidon seeking their food from the king's country in Acts 12:20.

Ellicott adds the geography that made the plan work. The "sea of Joppa" was the Jewish port to which the cedar was floated down the coast from Lebanon, and thence carried some thirty-five miles inland to Jerusalem; and the grant of Cyrus rested on his authority over Phoenicia, which seems not to have been doubtful. Matthew Henry lifts the arrangement into a word of trust: they applied themselves to this at once, for while we do what we can we must still be aiming to do more and better; Tyre and Sidon must now, as of old, furnish them with workmen, and Lebanon with timber, for both of which they had orders from Cyrus — and what God calls us to, he reminds us, we may depend upon his providence to furnish us for. The witnesses do not divide; together they show a poor and threatened remnant reaching back across five centuries to Solomon's very methods, and finding, in a pagan king's decree, the providence of God supplying what the work required.
8:
The narrative leaps forward to the following spring, and the witnesses read the second month of the second year as the moment the building itself was at last taken in hand. The reformed John Gill reconstructs the intervening months: the returning exiles had set out from Babylon in the spring of the preceding year, a journey of some four months as Ezra later performed it (Ezra 7:9); reaching Jerusalem in the seventh month they kept the feast of tabernacles, then went back to settle their own cities, the winter being no season to begin building, leaving workmen to clear the rubbish and ready the materials against the returning spring. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke confirms that the previous time had been spent clearing the ground, felling timber, hewing stones, and transporting them — the necessary preparation before a stone could be laid.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the formal commencement: in the second year of their coming to the house of God, in the second month, Zerubbabel and Jeshua and the remnant of their brethren began by appointing the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to oversee the work — that is, the building was now begun. Charles Ellicott fixes the date and finds a purpose in it: the second year of Cyrus, about B.C. 537, was their second year in the holy place; and the second month, Zif, was chosen apparently because it was the very month in which Solomon had laid his first foundation (1 Kings 6). The appointment of the Levites to superintend, and their specified age, he adds, are in strict harmony with the original ordinances of David (1 Chronicles 23).

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the timing and the men. There was no dispute among them whether to build; it was resolved on at once, and with all speed, for what comfort could they take in their own land without that token of God's presence? They took little more than half a year to prepare ground and materials, so much were their hearts upon it — and Henry draws the rule that when any good work is to be done it is our wisdom to set about it quickly, though we foresee difficulty and opposition, for "well begun is half ended." He marks too who began it — Zerubbabel and Jeshua and their brethren, magistrates and ministers and people all hearty for it — and finds it a good omen that God had given them one heart for the service. The witnesses do not divide; together they show a work resumed in the very month of Solomon's ancient beginning, ordered by David's old rule, and undertaken by a people of one mind who would not let a token of God's presence be long wanting.
9:
The verse names the Levite overseers who set the workmen forward, and the witnesses spend their labour on sorting out the men and their houses. The reformed John Gill issues the necessary caution at once: the Jeshua who "stood with his sons" here is not the high priest of the earlier verses but Jeshua the Levite, of whom Ezra 2:40 speaks. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley makes the same point — "not the high priest so called, but a Levite" — and reads their task, "to set forward the work," as encouraging the workmen to a vigorous prosecution of it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the three orders the verse enumerates: Jeshua with his sons and brethren; Kadmiel with his sons, called the sons of Judah; and the sons of Henadad with their sons and brethren. Jeshua and Kadmiel, they observe, are the two heads of Levitical orders already named in Ezra 2:40, and from comparing that passage they judge "sons of Judah" to be a clerical error for "sons of Hodaviah," a more precise designation of the sons of Kadmiel. The word rendered "together" they take as "all, without exception." Charles Ellicott reasons along the same lines: Jeshua and Kadmiel, both of the stock of Judah — or Hodaviah (Ezra 2:40), or Hodevah (Nehemiah 7:43) — were the two heads of Levitical families, and their fewness, he remarks, was compensated by their unanimity and vigour.

Over the sons of Henadad the witnesses register a small genuine puzzle without resolving it. Keil and Delitzsch note that this third class is not expressly named among those who returned from Babylon in Ezra 2:40; Ellicott presses the point, that Henadad is missing from that list though it is a Levitical name in Nehemiah, and confesses that why it should be omitted there, or inserted here, it is not possible to determine. The witnesses do not divide, and the very smallness of what they can settle is instructive. A handful of Levite families — three houses, and one of them of uncertain record — stand up "as one man" to marshal the labour on the house of God. Ellicott's remark holds the sense of it: the fewness of the overseers is made good by their singleness of mind. The work of rebuilding the temple, like the assembly that opened the chapter, goes forward not by numbers but by unanimity, a small and depleted Levitical remnant setting its whole weight, undivided, behind the workmen it was appointed to lead.
10:
Now the foundation is laid, and the witnesses turn to the solemn ceremonial that attended it — a service, they agree, deliberately modeled on the ancient ordinances. The reformed John Gill notes simply that the builders who laid the foundation were the masons, whose proper work it was. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the scene: when the foundation was laid, Zerubbabel and Joshua, the heads of the community, set the priests in their apparel — clothed, that is, in their robes of office (as at 2 Chronicles 5:12) — with trumpets, and the Levites the sons of Asaph with cymbals, to praise the LORD after the ordinance of David king of Israel.

The point on which the witnesses converge is that every element of the ceremony reached back to an appointed precedent. Charles Ellicott states it as a principle: all goes back to earlier times; as the first offerings on the altar were made according to what was "written in the law of Moses, the man of God," so the musical ceremonial of this foundation was according to the precedent of David (1 Chronicles 16). The trumpets belonged to the priests and the cymbals to the Levites, he adds, in the ancient ordinances of worship — the instruments assigned exactly as of old. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads "after the ordinance of David" to the same effect: the praise went up with the psalms David had composed, the people acting in the very manner he had directed.

Keil and Delitzsch record a difference among older expositors over how the singing was performed. Some — Clericus and J. H. Michaelis among them — referring to Exodus 15:21, understood the phrase as the alternate singing of two choirs, the one raising "Praise the LORD, for he is good" and the other answering "and his mercy endureth for ever." The matter belongs properly to the next verse, but it colours this one, for it shapes how the reader hears the praise that the trumpets and cymbals accompanied. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the sense of the whole: the priests with the trumpets appointed by Moses and the Levites with the cymbals appointed by David made up a concert of music, not to please the ear but to assist the singing of that everlasting hymn which will never be out of date. What the witnesses find in the verse is a foundation laid not in silence but in ordered praise — a poor and threatened remnant, raising the first stones of a diminished house, yet doing so exactly by the pattern of Moses and David, as though to bind the new work by every possible thread to the worship of the fathers.
11:
The praise breaks into antiphonal song, and the witnesses listen closely to how it was sung and what it said. The reformed John Gill explains "they sang together by course" as singing by turns, in responses, answering one another — when one company had performed its part, another took up theirs. Charles Ellicott says the same: they answered each other in chorus, antiphonally; and the great shout that followed was, as afterwards, a cry of religious acclamation. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that some older expositors, comparing Exodus 15:21, took the responsive singing quite literally: one choir sang out "Praise the LORD, for he is good," and the other answered "and his mercy endureth for ever."

The refrain itself draws the witnesses' warmest attention, for it is the burden of a psalm they all recognize. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley calls it "that everlasting hymn, which will never be out of date, and to which our tongue should never be out of tune" — the burden of Psalm 136; and he draws its lesson, that whatever our condition is, let it be owned that God is good, and, whatever fails, that his mercy fails not. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same hymn and presses its particular clause. The concert of trumpet and cymbal was raised, he says, not to please the ear but to assist the singing of that everlasting hymn to which our tongues should never be out of tune — "God is good, and his mercy endureth for ever." And he bids us sing it, as here, with application: not only does his mercy endure for ever, but it endures for ever toward Israel — Israel when captives in a strange land and strangers in their own; however it be, yet God is good to Israel (Psalm 73:1). Let the reviving of the church's interests, when they seemed dead, be ascribed to the continuance of that mercy, for therefore the church continues.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the mixture the verse first records — all the people shouted with a great shout, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid — a joy that the following verse will show was not the only note struck. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the antiphonal form; Keil and Delitzsch the ancient pattern of the responsive singing; Wesley and Henry the imperishable substance of the refrain. Together they render the sound of the moment: a diminished remnant, at the laying of a foundation far poorer than the house they had lost, lifting nonetheless the oldest confession of Israel's faith — that the LORD is good, and that his mercy, which had brought them home, endures toward his people for ever.
12:
Against the shouting rises another sound, and the witnesses gather around the old men who wept at what the younger ones cheered. The reformed John Gill fixes their age: the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers who wept were ancient men, seventy or eighty years old, old enough to have seen the first house before it fell. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that divers of them might well have seen it, since it had been destroyed not sixty years before; and he gathers the reasons for their tears — the poor preparations for this house compared with the former; its lack of the things that had been the first temple's chief glory, the ark and the Urim and Thummim; and the foundation-stones themselves, inferior to the old both in quantity and in price (1 Kings 7:9-10), and of a far narrower compass than the foundations of the whole first building.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke deepens the inventory of loss. The ancients saw that the glory had departed from Israel: they could not build such a house as the first, and even had it been possible it would have been greatly inferior, wanting the ark of the covenant, the heavenly fire, the mercy-seat, the manna, Aaron's rod that budded, the divine shechinah, the spirit of prophecy, and most probably the Urim and Thummim. Yet many shouted for joy — those who had not seen the original temple, and who rejoiced simply to be restored to their own land and to the worship of God in his own city. It must have been a very affecting sight, Clarke says: a whole people, one part crying aloud with sorrow, the other shouting aloud for joy, on the same occasion. And he points forward to the comfort the prophet Haggai would bring, that the glory of this latter house should exceed the former, because the Lord would come to it and fill it with his glory (Haggai 2:9).

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott qualifies the cause of the weeping. The first house had been destroyed some fifty years before, and the tears of the ancients, he judges, were not occasioned by any mere comparison of size and grandeur — unless indeed they marked the smallness of their foundation-stones — but by the thought of the great desolation as measured against the past, while the younger people thought rather of the new future; the whole scene, he adds, requires the comment of Haggai 2 and Zechariah 4. Matthew Henry holds the two sounds together with a pastor's balance: there was some reason for the tears, and if the old men bewailed the sin that was the cause of the melancholy change, they did well; yet it was their infirmity to mingle those tears with the common joys and cast a damp upon them, despising the day of small things and proving unthankful for the good they did enjoy, though it was far more than they deserved. The witnesses do not divide over the fact; they divide gently over the tears' worth, between a grief that rightly mourned a departed glory and a grief that wronged a present mercy.
13:
The chapter ends on a single, indistinguishable sound, and the witnesses attend to how the joy and the grief were blended past telling apart. The reformed John Gill takes the plain meaning: the people could not discern the shout of joy from the weeping, that is, not clearly and distinctly, for the two were so mixed and confounded together that they made a kind of jarring and discord. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch press the sense more exactly. The verse does not mean that the weeping of the old priests and Levites could not be heard because it was overpowered by the rejoicing of the multitude; rather it states that among the people at large, too — the assembly apart from the priests, Levites, and chiefs — both a shout of joy and a voice of weeping arose, but the shouting for joy was so loud that the sounds of rejoicing and weeping could not be told apart. The Hebrew verb, they note, means to perceive one thing in the presence of another, and so to distinguish the one from the other — the very thing the people here could not do.

Charles Ellicott reads the mingling the same way and vouches for its truth. The people also joined in the weeping, he says, which was with shrill cries; the rejoicing and the sorrow were blended, and the common sound was heard from far off. "All here," he adds, "has the stamp of truth" — the confused clamour of a great crowd, some exulting and some lamenting at once, is exactly what such a moment would have produced, and no invented scene would have been drawn so.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the blended noise into a parable of the world. This mixture of sorrow and joy, he says, is a representation of this present life: some are bathing in rivers of joy while others are drowned in floods of tears; and here on earth we can scarcely discern the shouts of joy from the noise of the weeping. In heaven all are singing and none sighing; in hell all are weeping and wailing and none rejoicing; but this world holds the two together, indistinguishably, as at the laying of this foundation. Let us learn, he urges from the apostle's rule in Romans 12:15, to rejoice with those that rejoice and weep with those that weep, and ourselves to rejoice as though we rejoiced not and to weep as though we wept not. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch fix the philology of the confused sound, Ellicott vouches for its unmistakable realism, Henry reads in it the very image of a world where joy and grief are never yet cleanly parted. The chapter that opened with a homeless people gathering "as one man" closes with that same people made one again — not now in a single resolve, but in a single cry, too full of both hope and loss to be untangled, and heard, undivided, a great way off.
